slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Stool (2–3 samples a few days apart; in preservative vials when needed)

What it is used for: The test shows whether intestinal parasites are causing symptoms of a gut infection and whether treatment is working. Such symptoms include diarrhea lasting a few days, belly pain, blood or mucus in stool, foul greasy floating stools, nausea, gas, fever and weight loss. It is more likely to be ordered with serious symptoms (dehydration), a weakened immune system, or possible exposure (untreated water, travel, contact with an infected person).

Physiology: Intestinal parasites live and reproduce in the digestive system; they and their eggs are passed in stool. Invisible traces of contaminated stool reach water, soil, food and surfaces, and infection follows when they are swallowed. Some worms, such as hookworms, enter through the skin, especially when walking barefoot.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: A wet mount shows protozoan trophozoites, cysts and oocysts as well as helminth eggs and larvae: a small amount of stool is placed on a slide and, if fairly solid, mixed with a drop or two of saline; ideally two smears are made on one slide, one stained with iodine. The whole coverslip is scanned systematically with the 10× objective. Permanent stained slides identify trophozoites and cysts to species — at least 200–300 oil-immersion fields are examined. Size is a key feature, so the microscope is calibrated with an ocular micrometer.

Direct (wet) microscopy is done in two drops: saline (warmed to 37 °C) shows motile trophozoites, Lugol’s iodine (iodine–acetic acid) shows cyst nuclei clearly — iodine immobilises trophozoites. Use liquid or mucoid stool for trophozoites and formed stool for eggs.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result
bullets: Positive result: A positive result means parasites and/or eggs were found — there are intestinal parasites. The report also gives the type and how many were seen. Treatment depends on the parasite and general health; plenty of fluids help prevent dehydration from diarrhea and vomiting.

Negative result: A negative result means no parasites or eggs were found: either there are none, or too few were in the sample. Parasites are not shed in stool every day, so collection is repeated after a negative first exam — CDC advises examining three specimens passed 2–3 days apart when possible.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/5
bullets: Pre-analytics: Collect stool in a dry, clean, leak-proof container with no urine, water or soil. Fresh stool is examined, processed or preserved immediately; an unpreserved specimen kept only under refrigeration is suitable for antigen testing only. Without a kit, the specimen is split between 10% formalin and PVA (polyvinyl alcohol): one volume of stool to three volumes of preservative, mixed well, with formed stool broken up.

Collect stool in a clean, dry, lidded container without preservative; no urine (not from a bedpan), and include any worms or segments passed. WHO advises examining it within 1–4 hours and, if several arrive together, looking first at liquid and blood- or mucus-stained stools — motile amoebae die quickly. Lyubina (1984) and Aripova (2007) also reject matchboxes or paper.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/5
bullets: For shipping to a distant laboratory a preservative is added: 10% formalin (for wet mounts and sedimentation), PVA (for permanent stains such as trichrome), MIF or SAF/TIF mixtures. Dadayev (2004) also notes that stool for amoebiasis must be preserved (or delivered quickly).

Interferences: Certain drugs and compounds make stool unsatisfactory for examination: antacids, kaolin, mineral oil and other oily materials, non-absorbable antidiarrheals, barium or bismuth (7–10 days to clear), antimicrobial agents (2–3 weeks) and gallbladder dyes (3 weeks). Collect before they are given or wait until their effects have passed.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/5
bullets: Limitations: Each preservative has drawbacks: formalin preserves helminth eggs, larvae and cysts well but not trophozoite morphology, and long fixation can interfere with PCR; PVA preserves trophozoites and cysts well but not helminth eggs or larvae, and is unsuitable for concentration procedures. Using both is therefore recommended. If PCR is needed, the specimen is collected to its specific requirements.
For pinworm, a stool test is usually not useful — stool rarely contains enough eggs; the perianal tape test is used instead.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 4/5
bullets: Concentration is needed when parasites are few. In flotation (e.g., Willis saturated NaCl; zinc sulfate) eggs rise in a dense solution: good for hookworm, Ascaris, Hymenolepis, Taenia and Trichuris eggs, but not for fluke and schistosome eggs, Strongyloides larvae or protozoa — some eggs do not float and cyst and egg walls may collapse. Sedimentation (formalin–ether or formalin–ethyl acetate) recovers more species, is easier, and CDC recommends it for general laboratories; ethyl acetate is less flammable than ether.

In the Kato (Kato–Katz) thick smear about 0.5 g of sieved stool is cleared under glycerol-soaked cellophane (with malachite green or methylene blue); it detects and counts helminth eggs, especially Schistosoma, and slides can be stored and shipped. It is unsuitable for strongyloidiasis, enterobiasis and protozoa.

slides.title: Stool ova and parasites (O&P)
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences · 5/5
bullets: No single method finds every parasite: always do direct microscopy before concentration (motile forms are not seen in concentrated preparations). If the result is negative, the doctor may request repeat samples on other days.

slides.title: Saline wet mount
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Motile trophozoites, moderate numbers of eggs and cysts, red cells, fat
Limitations: May miss scanty parasites; use liquid stool and saline warmed to 37 °C for trophozoites

slides.title: Iodine (Lugol) mount
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Cyst nuclei and glycogen vacuoles; telling Giardia and amoeba cysts apart
Limitations: Trophozoites stop moving — check motility in saline

slides.title: Kato (Kato–Katz) thick smear
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Helminth eggs, especially Schistosoma; egg counts; slides can be stored and shipped
Limitations: Not for strongyloidiasis, enterobiasis or protozoa

slides.title: Flotation
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Light eggs rise in a dense solution (saturated NaCl — Willis; zinc sulfate): hookworm, Ascaris, Hymenolepis, Taenia, Trichuris
Limitations: Fluke and schistosome eggs, Strongyloides larvae, protozoa; cyst and egg walls may collapse

slides.title: Sedimentation
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: What it finds: Formalin–ether or formalin–ethyl acetate: most eggs, larvae and cysts; CDC recommends it for general laboratories
Limitations: Motile forms are not seen — do a wet mount first; ether is flammable, ethyl acetate is safer

slides.title: Preservatives (shipping)
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: 10% formalin — for wet mounts and sedimentation; preserves eggs and cysts well, trophozoites less so.
PVA — for permanent (trichrome) stains; MIF, SAF or TIF — mixtures for wet mounts.
Fresh stool without preservative is examined within 1–4 hours; liquid and blood- or mucus-stained stool first.

slides.title: Pinworm: adhesive tape
slides.eyebrow: Tables and algorithms · Finding parasites in stool
bullets: Pinworm eggs are scarce in stool — collect them with tape from the perianal skin.
In the morning before washing or using the toilet; repeat on three consecutive days.

slides.title: Tapeworms (Cestoda): structure
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 1/2
bullets: Tapeworms (cestodes) are endoparasites: sexually mature worms live in many vertebrates, including the human intestine, and a few species in other organs; the body is flattened dorsoventrally and has no body cavity.
The body consists of a head (scolex), a neck and segments (proglottids); the neck is the growth zone where young segments form.
The scolex has attachment organs: suckers (in some also hooks) or, in the broad tapeworm, bothria (deep grooves).
The digestive system is reduced: nutrients from digested food in the gut are absorbed through the whole body surface.

Sex organs are repeated in every segment (hermaphroditic); in the beef-tapeworm example they develop fully at about the 200th segment from the neck, and the last mature segments consist of a uterus filled with fertilised eggs.

slides.title: Tapeworms (Cestoda): structure
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 2/2
bullets: Mature segments detach from the strobila and leave with the faeces; strobilation (formation of segments) continues throughout the parasite’s life.

slides.title: Development cycle of cestodes
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 1/2
bullets: Cestodes are biohelminths: in the development cycle, besides the definitive host, one or two intermediate hosts take part.
Eggs leave the host’s intestine with faeces and proglottids; inside the egg a six-hooked embryo — the oncosphere (in some a ten-hooked larva, the lycophore) — develops.

For further development the egg must be swallowed by an intermediate host; in its gut the oncosphere leaves the shell, pierces the gut wall with its hooks, enters blood or lymph vessels and settles in an organ (liver, lung, heart, brain, muscle).
There the oncosphere turns into the second, bladder-like larval stage — the finna (larvocyst); finnae are of five types: cysticercus, coenurus, echinococcus, cysticercoid and plerocercoid.

slides.title: Development cycle of cestodes
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 2/2
bullets: If the definitive host swallows meat of the intermediate host containing finnae, in its gut the scolex everts from the bladder and attaches to the gut wall, the bladder disappears and young segments begin to form from the neck.
Depending on the number of worms in the host’s gut they are fertilised in different ways: with a single worm, segments may fertilise one another or themselves.

slides.title: Beef, pork and fish tapeworms
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 1/2
bullets: Beef tapeworm (Taeniarhynchus saginatus): lives in the human small intestine, 4–10 m long; the scolex has 4 suckers and no hooks (“unarmed”); mature segments have 18–35 lateral uterine branches on each side; intermediate host — cattle, larva — cysticercus (finna); humans are infected by eating raw or undercooked meat containing finnae; the disease is taeniarhynchosis.

Pork tapeworm (Taenia solium): 1.5–3 m long (sometimes up to 5 m), up to 900 segments; the scolex has 4 suckers and two rows of hooks (22–32) on the rostellum — “armed”; 7–12 lateral uterine branches; intermediate host — pig (also dog, cat, camel, rabbit), larva — cysticercus.

slides.title: Beef, pork and fish tapeworms
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 2/2
bullets: With the pork tapeworm a human can be not only the definitive but also an intermediate host: oncospheres from eggs, or from segments that rise from the gut into the stomach, enter organs (eye, brain, heart, muscle) and cause cysticercosis — finnosis; autoinvasion is possible; the diseases are taeniasis and cysticercosis.
Broad (fish) tapeworm (Diphyllobothrium latum): the largest, 10–15 m long, up to 4000 segments; the scolex has two bothria instead of suckers; eggs develop in water; the uterus is rosette-shaped.

The broad tapeworm has 3 hosts: definitive — humans and carnivorous mammals; first intermediate — small crustaceans (copepods), larva — procercoid; second intermediate — fish, larva — plerocercoid; humans are infected through raw or undercooked fish or roe; the disease is diphyllobothriasis, in which anaemia may develop.

slides.title: Methods of finding large helminths and segments in stool
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 1/2
bullets: Fresh stool samples are usually examined by eye to find parasitic worms or worm segments visible to the naked eye.

Macroscopic method: stool is stirred with water to a liquid consistency, small portions are placed in a black photographic tray or a Petri dish on a black background and examined by eye or with a hand lens (20× magnification); a suspicious piece is examined between two slides in a drop of glycerol.

Sedimentation method: stool pieces collected after an anthelmintic or laxative are put into a large vessel, washed under a strong stream of water and left to settle (helminths sink); the sediment is washed repeatedly until the water is clear, then examined on a black background.

slides.title: Methods of finding large helminths and segments in stool
slides.eyebrow: Short summary from the textbook · 2/2
bullets: The “sieving” method is used to find large helminths (ascarids, whipworm, large tapeworms): stool is washed with water in a set of 3–4 metal sieves and the helminths are retained on the sieves; it is unsuitable for small helminths.
Direct wet-mount technique is used to find eggs, larvae, trophozoites and cysts; for motile trophozoites a fresh stool sample is essential.
Quality control in parasitology depends on standardised methods and staff skills: the laboratory should keep positive control slides or illustrations against which the parasites found are compared.

slides.title: A patient had a barium x-ray yesterday and today's stool is sent for parasites. What is right?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Q&A
options: Wait until the barium effect clears (7–10 days), then collect
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct. Collect before barium or after its effects have passed.

Basis: CDC DPDx: barium or bismuth makes stool unsatisfactory; 7–10 days are needed for the effect to clear.

slides.title: Biology, morphology, laboratory diagnosis of tapeworms?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline
bullets: 1. Cestodes are tape-like hermaphroditic worms: scolex, neck, proglottids (strobila); no intestinal cavity.

2. Main species: Taenia saginata (cattle), T. solium (pig; risk of cysticercosis if eggs are ingested), Hymenolepis nana (may be transmitted without an intermediate host), Diphyllobothrium, Echinococcus (humans are an intermediate host).
3. Laboratory: eggs in stool (Taenia eggs 30–35 µm, radially striated, T. solium and T. saginata cannot be distinguished), examination of proglottids.
4. Species identification: number of uterine branches in the proglottid, structure of the scolex; molecular methods.
5. In echinococcosis and cysticercosis – imaging and serology; taeniid eggs may be infectious – precautions.

slides.title: Macro- and microscopy of tapeworms?
slides.eyebrow: Practice · Answer outline
bullets: 1. Macroscopy: proglottids passed in stool – press between two glass slides and count the uterine branches (more in T. saginata, fewer in T. solium).
2. Scolex: T. solium – with hooklets (armed), T. saginata – without hooklets; Hymenolepis is small.
3. Microscopy: eggs in stool (wet mount, enrichment); Taenia eggs 30–35 µm, with a thick radially striated embryophore, inside an oncosphere with 6 hooklets.
4. Hymenolepis nana egg – thin-shelled, with filaments at the poles; H. diminuta – larger, without filaments.
5. Caution: T. solium proglottids and eggs are infectious to humans – gloves, decontamination.
